placeholders.name: YOUR NICHE, e.g. "budgeting and money management for freelancers"
placeholders.what: This is the specific subject plus angle you make content about, described the way you'd say it to a stranger in one sentence — not just a broad topic like "fitness" or "finance." Use the same wording you'd put in your bio or channel description. A good value has a clear wedge (who it's for or what makes your take different); a bad value is one generic word.
examples: budgeting and money management for freelancers
strength training for women over 40 returning to the gym after a break
sourdough baking for people who travel a lot and can't maintain a daily starter

placeholders.name: WHO, e.g. "new freelancers 1-3 years in, anxious about irregular income"
placeholders.what: Describe the specific segment of people you're making this for — their experience level, a specific fear or goal, or life stage — not just "freelancers" or "women." Pull this from your platform analytics demographics or from the pattern of people who actually comment and DM you, not a guess at who you wish was watching.
examples: new freelancers 1-3 years in, anxious about irregular income and afraid to raise their rates
moms of toddlers who used to lift weights in college and want to get back into it without hurting themselves
home bakers who bought a starter once, let it die, and feel guilty trying again

placeholders.name: PASTE 3-5 EXAMPLES OR WRITE "no data yet"
placeholders.what: List past pieces of content that clearly outperformed your average, with the title/topic and a short honest guess at why it worked. Pull real numbers from your platform analytics if you have them. If you're new and have no track record, write "no data yet" literally — that stops the AI from inventing a pattern that doesn't exist.
examples:
"Why I stopped tracking every invoice in a spreadsheet" (short-form video, 40K views) — worked because it admitted failure before giving the fix
"The $3,200 mistake I made my first year freelancing" (newsletter) — worked because of the specific dollar figure in the subject line
"3 clients who ghosted me and what I do differently now" (carousel) — worked because it was a relatable list post with concrete numbers
no data yet

"Deadlift form check: the mistake I see in every gym" (Reel, 120K views) — worked because it called out a mistake viewers could self-diagnose
"I took 6 months off lifting, here's what came back and what didn't" (YouTube, 15 min) — worked because it was an honest personal update, not a tutorial

placeholders.name: PASTE REAL QUESTIONS, COMMENTS, OR DMs
placeholders.what: Paste actual verbatim text from comments, DMs, or emails from your real audience — not a summary or paraphrase. Scroll the comments on your last 5-10 posts, check saved DMs, or search your email for recurring reader questions. Keeping their exact wording (typos and all) matters because it shows real phrasing your audience uses, which makes the ideas land better.
examples:
"how do you know how much to charge when you're just starting out??"
"I have 3 clients paying wildly different rates for the same work, is that normal"
"do you ever just... not invoice someone because you feel bad"
"what do you do in the months where literally nothing comes in"

"is it too late to start lifting at 45"
"my knees click when I squat, should I stop"
"how long till I feel as strong as before having kids"

"my starter smells like nail polish remover, did I kill it"
"can I put it in the fridge for 2 weeks while I'm on a trip"
"why does everyone's bread look better than mine, mine's always flat"

placeholders.name: e.g., short-form video, long-form YouTube, newsletter, carousel posts
placeholders.what: List only the formats you actually currently publish in, with rough length/platform if it matters — not formats you wish you made. This keeps the AI from suggesting a 20-minute documentary idea when you only have a pipeline for 30-second clips.
examples: short-form video (Reels/TikTok, 30-60 sec), weekly newsletter
long-form YouTube (10-15 min), Instagram carousel posts, short-form video
podcast episodes (25-40 min), show notes newsletter, 3 short-form clips per episode

variations.label: Fast weekly top-up
variations.whenToUse: Use this on a normal week when you just need a quick refill of ideas for your existing content calendar, not a full strategic batch — e.g. a 10-minute Monday planning session.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me build a quick weekly content idea top-up. Do not give me generic ideas anyone in this niche could post — every idea must connect to a specific detail I give you below.

My niche: [YOUR NICHE]
My audience: [WHO]
Recurring questions/comments from my audience this week: [PASTE REAL QUESTIONS, COMMENTS, OR DMs]
Formats I create in: [YOUR FORMATS]

Generate 6 content ideas, each with: a specific title/hook (not a vague topic), which of my inputs it's grounded in, and the best format for it. Keep it fast — no long explanations, just the list.

variations.label: Trend-aware batch
variations.whenToUse: Use when you want ideas that also account for what's currently trending in your niche or what competitors are covering right now, without directly copying anyone.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me build a content idea list that's grounded in my own audience data but also aware of what's happening right now in my niche. Do not give me generic ideas — every idea must connect to a specific detail I give you below.

My niche: [YOUR NICHE]
My audience: [WHO]
My best-performing past content: [PAST HITS OR "no data yet"]
Recurring questions/comments from my audience: [PASTE REAL QUESTIONS, COMMENTS, OR DMs]
What's trending in my niche right now or what competitors are covering: [PASTE TRENDING TOPICS OR COMPETITOR CONTENT YOU'VE NOTICED]
Formats I create in: [YOUR FORMATS]

Generate 15 ideas, each with a specific hook, which input it's grounded in, and a flag for whether it's timely (should go out this week) or evergreen (can wait). Don't suggest anything that would just be copying a competitor's exact angle — my ideas need my own audience's questions or my own past hits as the anchor.

variations.label: Single-pillar deep dive
variations.whenToUse: Use when you already know one content pillar you want to focus a whole month on, rather than getting variety across all your pillars.
variations.prompt:
You are helping me build a deep, focused content idea list for one specific pillar of my niche. Do not give me generic ideas anyone in this niche could post — every idea must connect to a specific detail I give you below.

My niche: [YOUR NICHE]
The one pillar I want to focus on this month: [NAME THE PILLAR, e.g. "pricing and rate negotiation"]
My audience: [WHO]
Recurring questions/comments related to this pillar: [PASTE REAL QUESTIONS, COMMENTS, OR DMs]
Formats I create in: [YOUR FORMATS]

Generate 15 ideas, all within this one pillar, but make sure each explores a genuinely different angle (a myth to debunk, a personal story, a step-by-step, a comparison, a mistake to flag) so it doesn't feel repetitive across a month of posting. For each, note the angle and which input it's grounded in.

followUps.label: Cut ideas that aren't actually traceable
followUps.prompt: Look back through your list and remove any idea where the traceability to my inputs feels like a stretch. For the ones you keep, quote the exact phrase from my inputs above each idea is grounded in.

followUps.label: Push for sharper hooks
followUps.prompt: Some of these titles are still too safe or generic. Rewrite the 5 weakest hooks to be more specific, using a number, a contradiction, or a named mistake instead of a general statement.

followUps.label: Prioritize into a shortlist
followUps.prompt: From all 20 ideas, pick the 5 I should make first. Rank them by a combination of how proven the input is (a past hit beats a guess) and how fast I could realistically produce it, and explain why each ranks where it does.

followUps.label: Add a production note
followUps.prompt: For the top 5 you just picked, add one line each on what I'd actually need to produce it — b-roll, an interview, a screen recording, data I'd need to look up — so I know what's involved before committing.

cre-b1-idea-generation-system.walkthrough:
Dana runs a small Instagram and newsletter about budgeting for freelancers. She opens Claude and pastes the idea-generation prompt. For "my niche" she writes "budgeting and money management for freelancers." For "my audience" she writes "new freelancers 1-3 years in, anxious about irregular income." She has no analytics dashboard handy, so for past hits she just types "no data yet." She opens her Instagram app, scrolls her last few posts' comments, and copies four real comments word for word, including "do you ever just... not invoice someone because you feel bad." For formats she writes "short-form video, weekly newsletter."

Claude replies with 20 ideas grouped under the three headers. Under "Answers a question my audience already asked," the first idea is: "The Invoice I Almost Didn't Send (And What It Cost Me)" — grounded directly in her pasted comment about feeling bad invoicing people, flagged as better suited to a personal story than a how-to.

Dana sends the follow-up "Prioritize into a shortlist" because 20 ideas feel overwhelming and she only has time to film one video this week. Claude ranks the top 5, putting the invoice story first because it's grounded in a real, recent comment and needs no research — just her talking to camera.

Dana copies that top idea into her notes app and starts scripting that afternoon. The whole session, from opening Claude to having a ranked shortlist, took about 12 minutes — faster than the 45 minutes she usually spent staring at a blank notes doc trying to think of something to post.

placeholders.name: PASTE 100-200 WORDS OF YOUR OWN WRITING OR A TRANSCRIPT OF YOU TALKING
placeholders.what: An actual sample of you writing or speaking — a past caption, an auto-generated transcript from one of your videos, or an email you sent — long enough (100-200 words) for the AI to detect your real sentence length and word choices. This must be a genuine sample, not a description like "I'm casual and funny," which is an instruction, not evidence.
examples: So okay here's the thing nobody tells you about pricing your first client project — you're going to lowball it. Everyone does. I quoted $400 for a logo package that ended up taking me 30 hours, and I remember doing the math in the shower and just laughing because I made less than minimum wage. But here's what I did after that one job that actually changed things. I started asking one question before I ever sent a quote, and it's saved me probably ten thousand dollars since.

Look, I'm not going to sugarcoat this: your first six months back in the gym after having a kid are going to feel humiliating if you compare yourself to before. I had a client last week nearly cry because she couldn't squat the bar empty. That's not weakness. That's your body having done something extraordinary and now needing to rebuild. So we're not chasing your old numbers. We're building new ones, and I'll show you exactly how.

People ask me constantly why their starter died and honestly 90% of the time it's the same reason — you fed it once, panicked when it didn't double in size after 4 hours, and threw it out. Starters are slow. They're not sourdough-Instagram slow. Give it a week before you give up on it, and stop judging it against someone else's jar.

placeholders.name: YOUR IDEA/HOOK
placeholders.what: The specific content idea this script or outline is for, ideally lifted straight from an idea you already generated (from your idea list or a comment you're responding to) rather than a vague topic like "pricing tips."
examples: The $3,200 mistake I made my first year freelancing
Deadlift form check: the mistake I see in every gym
Why your sourdough starter isn't the problem, your schedule is

placeholders.name: short-form video script / long-form video script / written post outline / newsletter outline
placeholders.what: Pick exactly one of these four options — whichever this specific piece is actually being made for — and replace the whole slash-separated list with just that one choice.
examples: short-form video script
newsletter outline
long-form video script

placeholders.name: LIST 2-5 POINTS
placeholders.what: The specific facts, steps, or story beats that must appear somewhere in the finished piece, written as short notes in your own words — not a full script. This is what keeps the AI from inventing claims or missing the actual point you wanted to make.
examples: 1) I quoted way too low on my first project, 2) the exact question I now ask before quoting, 3) how I raised rates without losing the client, 4) the one line I say when a client pushes back
1) form breakdown of the mistake (hips rising early), 2) why it happens (weak posterior chain), 3) the one cue that fixed it for me, 4) when to deload instead of pushing through
1) most starters aren't actually dead, 2) the 3 signs it's really dead vs just sluggish, 3) how to revive a sluggish one in 48 hours

placeholders.name: e.g., 60 seconds spoken / 800 words / 5 outline sections
placeholders.what: How long the finished piece should be, in units that match the format you chose — seconds for a spoken video, words for written pieces, number of sections for an outline. Without a concrete target the AI defaults to a generic length that may not fit your platform's actual runtime or attention span.
examples: 45 seconds spoken
900 words
6 outline sections

variations.label: Series version
variations.whenToUse: Use when one idea is big enough to become a 2-3 part series and you want each part scripted with its own hook while still feeling connected.
variations.prompt:
Here is a sample of my own writing/speaking voice:
[PASTE 100-200 WORDS OF YOUR OWN WRITING OR A TRANSCRIPT OF YOU TALKING]

Match this voice exactly — including sentence length, how formal or casual I am, and words I'd actually use. Do not add hype phrases like "let's dive in," "game-changer," or "in today's video" unless they appear in my sample.

Content idea: [YOUR IDEA/HOOK]
This is a [2 or 3]-part series. Format: [short-form video script / long-form video script / written post outline / newsletter outline]
Key points across the whole series: [LIST 2-5 POINTS, noting which part each belongs to]
Length target per part: [e.g., 60 seconds spoken each]

Write all parts. Give each part its own hook in the first 3 seconds that stands alone even if someone hasn't seen the earlier parts, but end each part (except the last) with a specific reason to watch the next one. Do not introduce a new angle or claim I didn't ask for.

variations.label: Responding to someone else's words
variations.whenToUse: Use when the piece is a duet, reply, or response to a specific comment or another creator's clip, and that other person's words need to be woven in accurately.
variations.prompt:
Here is a sample of my own writing/speaking voice:
[PASTE 100-200 WORDS OF YOUR OWN WRITING OR A TRANSCRIPT OF YOU TALKING]

Match this voice exactly — including sentence length, how formal or casual I am, and words I'd actually use. Do not add hype phrases unless they appear in my sample.

What I'm responding to (paste their exact words): [PASTE THE COMMENT OR CLIP TRANSCRIPT YOU'RE RESPONDING TO]
My actual take on it: [YOUR IDEA/HOOK]
Format: [short-form video script / long-form video script / written post outline / newsletter outline]
Key points I want covered: [LIST 2-5 POINTS]
Length target: [e.g., 60 seconds spoken]

Write the script/outline. Quote or paraphrase what I'm responding to accurately in the first few seconds so it's clear what I'm reacting to, then move into my take. Do not put words in the other person's mouth that they didn't say.

variations.label: Voice style-guide only
variations.whenToUse: Use the first time you try this system, before writing anything, to get a written description of your voice back so you can sanity-check it and reuse it as a reference.
variations.prompt:
Here is a sample of my own writing/speaking voice:
[PASTE 100-200 WORDS OF YOUR OWN WRITING OR A TRANSCRIPT OF YOU TALKING]

Don't write any content yet. Instead, analyze this sample and give me a short voice style guide: typical sentence length, how formal or casual I am, words/phrases I actually use, words or phrases I'd never say (like generic hype phrases), and how I typically open a piece. I'll reuse this guide alongside future scripts.

followUps.label: Flag anything that still sounds like AI
followUps.prompt: Read this back and highlight every phrase that sounds more like generic AI writing than something I'd actually say out loud. Rewrite just those phrases to match my sample voice.

followUps.label: Tighten the hook
followUps.prompt: The first line needs to be stronger. Give me 3 alternative hooks in my voice, each testing a different angle (a question, a bold claim, jumping into the middle of the story).

followUps.label: Check length against target
followUps.prompt: Read this out loud at a natural speaking pace (or count the words) and tell me the actual length. If it's over my target, cut it down without losing any of my key points.

followUps.label: Verify nothing extra was added
followUps.prompt: Go through this line by line and flag any claim or detail that wasn't in my key points list. I want to check nothing was invented, and if something was added, tell me exactly where.

cre-b2-scripts-outlines-own-voice.walkthrough:
Priya makes fitness content for women returning to lifting after having kids. She opens ChatGPT and pastes the voice-matching prompt. For her voice sample, she copies a caption from a post that did well: "Look, I'm not going to sugarcoat this: your first six months back in the gym after having a kid are going to feel humiliating if you compare yourself to before..."

For content idea she writes "Deadlift form check: the mistake I see in every gym." Format: "short-form video script." Key points: "1) form breakdown of the mistake — hips rising early, 2) why it happens — weak posterior chain, 3) the one cue that fixed it for me." Length target: "45 seconds spoken."

ChatGPT returns a script opening with "If your squat breaks down here, it's not your legs" and continuing in short, direct sentences matching her sample, ending with the cue she gave it.

Priya reads it out loud once and it runs closer to 65 seconds, so she sends the follow-up "Check length against target." ChatGPT trims two sentences that repeated the same point twice and confirms the new version lands at about 44 seconds when spoken normally.

She copies the trimmed script into her teleprompter app and films it that evening. From opening ChatGPT to having a shootable script took about 9 minutes, and unlike scripts she'd written from scratch before, she didn't need to rewrite any lines to sound like herself — she only changed one word before filming.

placeholders.name: video transcript / article / newsletter
placeholders.what: State which one of these three source types you're pasting below — this tells the AI whether to expect spoken, conversational structure (a transcript) or written prose (an article/newsletter), which changes how it splits the content into posts.
examples: video transcript
article
newsletter

placeholders.name: PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT
placeholders.what: Paste the entire piece here, not a summary — every fact, number, and claim the AI is allowed to reuse across the 10 posts has to actually be visible in this text, not something you remember being in it. Get this from your video's auto-generated transcript (export from YouTube Studio or a tool like Descript) or the full published text of your article/newsletter.
examples: Most freelancers think pricing is the hard part. It's not. The hard part is the conversation you have with yourself at 2am after a client says 'can you do it for less'... [continues for 1,400 words through 6 sections on rate-setting, client conversations, and a personal story about a $3,200 underquote]

[Full YouTube transcript, ~1,800 words, of a talking-head video titled 'Why your squat form breaks down at heavier weight,' covering hip drive, bracing technique, and 3 common coaching cues, with timestamps from the auto-caption export]

[Full newsletter text, ~900 words, titled 'The starter isn't dead, your schedule is,' including a personal anecdote about almost throwing out a 3-year-old starter, 3 diagnostic questions, and a 48-hour revival routine]

placeholders.name: ONE SENTENCE
placeholders.what: The single core idea every one of the 10 posts must trace back to, written as one clear sentence. This is the throughline that keeps 10 separate posts feeling like one coherent piece of content instead of 10 unrelated fragments pulled from the same source.
examples: Most freelancers underprice because they've never been taught to separate 'what I'd charge a friend' from 'what the market actually pays.'
Your squat form breaks down at heavier weight because of a bracing problem, not a mobility problem.
A sourdough starter that seems dead is almost always just sluggish from an inconsistent feeding schedule, not actually dead.

variations.label: Single-platform deep batch
variations.whenToUse: Use when you only need posts for one platform this week — for example 10 Instagram Reel ideas from one piece — rather than a spread across formats.
variations.prompt:
Here is my source content, a [video transcript / article / newsletter]:
[PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT]

Core idea I want preserved across everything: [ONE SENTENCE]

Repurpose this into 10 short-form video scripts for one platform, not a mix of formats. Do not just shorten or copy-paste sections — genuinely reformat each one as its own standalone hook/angle on the core idea, while keeping every fact and claim traceable to the source above (do not add new information).

For each of the 10 scripts, include: the hook line, the full spoken script (under 45 seconds each), a [VISUAL: ...] cue for each beat, and which specific part of the source it's drawn from. Vary the hooks across all 10 — no two should open the same way or use the same structure (question, bold claim, mid-story, myth-bust, etc.).

variations.label: Evergreen vs timely split
variations.whenToUse: Use when the source content mixes timeless advice with something time-sensitive (a trend, a recent event, a seasonal detail) and you want the repurposed posts organized by how long they stay relevant.
variations.prompt:
Here is my source content, a [video transcript / article / newsletter]:
[PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT]

Core idea I want preserved across everything: [ONE SENTENCE]

Repurpose this into 10 platform-native posts, following the same format mix as usual (short-form scripts, carousel outlines, captions, LinkedIn-style posts, newsletter blurb). Do not add new information beyond the source.

Additionally, sort all 10 posts into two groups: "Evergreen — post anytime" and "Timely — post within the next 2 weeks while still relevant," based on whether the post references anything time-sensitive from the source. For each post, note which specific part of the source it's drawn from.

variations.label: Fast subset for a light week
variations.whenToUse: Use when you only have capacity to produce 3-4 repurposed posts this week instead of the full 10, and want the highest-leverage ones first.
variations.prompt:
Here is my source content, a [video transcript / article / newsletter]:
[PASTE FULL SOURCE TEXT]

Core idea I want preserved across everything: [ONE SENTENCE]

I only have time to produce 4 posts this week. Recommend the 4 highest-leverage platform-native posts from this source — mix of formats is fine, your call — that each stand alone without requiring the full source piece for context. For each: the format, the full post/script, which part of the source it's drawn from, and one sentence on why you picked it over the other possible angles.

followUps.label: Check nothing was invented
followUps.prompt: Go through all 10 posts and flag any fact, number, or claim that doesn't appear in my source text. I need to confirm nothing was added before I publish any of these.

followUps.label: Vary the hooks more
followUps.prompt: A few of these hooks open too similarly. Rewrite the openings so no two of the 10 start with the same sentence structure or word.

followUps.label: Pick today's best 3
followUps.prompt: I can only produce 3 of these this week. Recommend which 3 to prioritize based on which best stand alone without needing the full source piece for context, and explain why.

followUps.label: Tighten short-form scripts to true spoken length
followUps.prompt: Read the 3 short-form video scripts out loud at a natural pace and tell me if any run over 45 seconds. Cut whichever ones do without losing the hook or the core idea.

cre-i1-repurpose-one-piece-ten-posts.walkthrough:
Marcus writes a weekly newsletter about freelance pricing. He just published a 900-word issue and wants to stretch it further instead of writing something new from scratch. He opens Claude and pastes the repurposing prompt.

For the source type he writes "newsletter," then pastes the full 900-word text, including the anecdote about underquoting a client by $3,200. For the core idea he writes one sentence: "Most freelancers underprice because they've never been taught to separate 'what I'd charge a friend' from 'what the market actually pays.'"

Claude returns all 10 pieces. The first short-form script opens with "I lost $3,200 by being nice" and uses [VISUAL: hands typing an invoice, then deleting a number] as a cue. A carousel outline breaks the newsletter's 3-question pricing framework into 6 slides, one question per slide plus an intro and closer. Each item lists which paragraph of the newsletter it pulled from.

Marcus reads through and notices two of the three short-form scripts both open with a question, so he sends the follow-up "Vary the hooks more." Claude rewrites one to open mid-story instead: "So I'm doing the math in the shower, and I start laughing, because I just realized I made less than minimum wage."

Marcus copies the reworked scripts, carousel outline, and captions into his content calendar. The whole session took about 20 minutes, and he came away with a week and a half of posts from one newsletter he'd already written — instead of the usual scramble to think of something new each day.

placeholders.name: YOUR TITLE OR HOOK
placeholders.what: The exact title or on-thumbnail text you plan to publish with this piece, so the image composition and its empty space work together with the real words that will sit on top of it. Use your actual planned title, not a placeholder like "my video title."
examples: The $3,200 mistake I made my first year freelancing
Your squat form breaks down for this ONE reason
I killed my starter (here's how I brought it back)

placeholders.name: e.g., YouTube 16:9, Instagram 1:1, Pinterest 2:3
placeholders.what: The exact platform and aspect ratio/pixel dimensions the image needs to be built for. GPT Image 2 composes differently depending on the canvas shape, and each platform crops or displays images differently, so this has to be specific, not just "a thumbnail."
examples: YouTube thumbnail, 16:9, 1280x720px
Instagram feed post, 1:1, 1080x1080px
Pinterest pin, 2:3, 1000x1500px

placeholders.name: e.g., curious, urgent, calm, surprised
placeholders.what: The single primary emotion you want someone to feel in the half-second they glance at this image while scrolling — this drives facial expression, color intensity, and composition tension. Pick one dominant emotion, not a list of several, or the result will come out muddled.
examples: urgent, slightly alarmed
curious, a little confused
calm, reassured

placeholders.name: YOUR COLORS, e.g., "warm oranges and cream, minimal, one clear subject"
placeholders.what: Your actual established brand colors and style, taken from your channel banner, logo, or past thumbnails — not colors that would just look nice for this one image. Staying consistent across every thumbnail is what makes your channel instantly recognizable in someone's feed.
examples: warm oranges and cream, minimal, one clear subject
navy blue and bright yellow, bold, high-contrast
sage green and terracotta, soft, slightly muted tones

placeholders.name: left/right/center
placeholders.what: A single-word choice: which third of the frame the main subject should sit in. GPT Image 2's composition planning follows this instruction precisely, so it determines where the empty space for your text overlay ends up — pick it based on where your channel usually places text.
examples: left
right
center

placeholders.name: e.g., "photographic, not illustrated" or "flat vector illustration" — be specific, don't leave it generic
placeholders.what: The specific rendering style GPT Image 2 should use — name a concrete photography type, illustration technique, or specific art reference, not a vague word like "nice" or "eye-catching," which produces a generic-looking result.
examples: photographic, natural light, shot like an iPhone photo, not a polished studio shoot
flat vector illustration, 2-color palette, like a modern editorial icon
photorealistic, dramatic side lighting, shallow depth of field

variations.label: Batch across several upcoming titles
variations.whenToUse: Use when planning thumbnails for several upcoming videos at once, so they stay visually consistent as a set instead of designed one at a time in isolation.
variations.prompt:
Generate thumbnail/cover image concepts for a batch of upcoming pieces, keeping a consistent visual system across all of them.

Titles/hooks: [LIST YOUR UPCOMING TITLES, ONE PER LINE]
Platform and dimensions: [e.g., YouTube 16:9]
Brand style (must stay identical across all): [YOUR COLORS]
Composition rule (must stay identical across all): one clear focal point in the [left/right/center] third, leaving negative space in the opposite third for a text overlay.
Style reference: [e.g., "photographic, not illustrated"]

For each title, generate one concept with its own mood/emotion suited to that specific title, but keep the color palette, composition rule, and style reference identical across every one so the set reads as one channel when displayed side by side.

variations.label: A/B headline test
variations.whenToUse: Use when you want to test two different text-overlay headlines on the same visual concept to see which one performs better before committing.
variations.prompt:
Generate one thumbnail/cover image concept, then show it with two different headline options for me to A/B test.

Topic: [YOUR TITLE OR HOOK]
Headline option A (on-image text): [HEADLINE A]
Headline option B (on-image text): [HEADLINE B]
Platform and dimensions: [e.g., YouTube 16:9]
Mood/emotion: [e.g., curious, urgent]
Brand style: [YOUR COLORS]
Composition: one clear focal point in the [left/right/center] third, leaving negative space in the opposite third for the text overlay.
Style reference: [e.g., "photographic, not illustrated"]

Generate one image concept only, but describe how the negative space would accommodate each headline option (line breaks, font size) since option A and B are different lengths. Avoid warped text, generic stock-photo people, and more than one focal subject.

variations.label: Reusable series template
variations.whenToUse: Use when designing a repeatable visual template for a recurring content series (same layout and colors every episode) rather than a one-off thumbnail.
variations.prompt:
Design a reusable thumbnail template concept for a recurring series, not a one-off image.

Series name: [YOUR SERIES NAME, e.g. "Form Check Friday"]
What changes each episode: [e.g., "the subject/exercise being demonstrated"]
What must stay identical every episode: [e.g., "the color palette, the badge/logo placement, the font style for text overlay"]
Platform and dimensions: [e.g., YouTube 16:9]
Brand style: [YOUR COLORS]
Composition: one clear focal point in the [left/right/center] third, leaving negative space in the opposite third for text overlay, kept identical every episode.
Style reference: [e.g., "photographic, not illustrated"]

Describe the template as a fixed formula I can hand to myself or an editor every week: what stays fixed, what's the one variable element, and generate one example using this week's topic: [THIS WEEK'S TITLE].

followUps.label: Simplify a too-busy result

cre-i2-thumbnails-visuals-ai-image.walkthrough:
Elena makes YouTube videos about strength training for women over 40. She's about to publish a video titled "Your squat form breaks down for this ONE reason" and needs a thumbnail. She opens ChatGPT and pastes the thumbnail prompt into a new chat, since GPT Image 2 is available directly in the composer.

She fills in: topic "Your squat form breaks down for this ONE reason," platform "YouTube, 16:9, 1280x720px," mood "urgent, slightly alarmed," brand style "navy blue and bright yellow, bold, high-contrast" (pulled from her channel banner), composition "left" since she always puts her bold yellow text on the right side of her thumbnails, and style reference "photographic, natural light, shot like an iPhone photo, not a polished studio shoot."

ChatGPT generates 3 variations: subject on the left with clean negative space on the right, subject on the right, and subject centered. Because she specified "left," that version matches her usual layout best — a woman mid-squat, weight visibly loaded, expression focused, with a clean navy gradient background on the right third, and the negative space genuinely empty since she told GPT Image 2 not to render her title text.

Elena sends the follow-up "Check readability at small size" because she remembers a past thumbnail that looked great full-size but got muddy once shrunk down in search results. ChatGPT tells her the centered version's subject gets too small to read at thumbnail size, while the left-aligned version holds up because the subject fills more of its third.

She picks the left-aligned version, adds her yellow bold text over the empty right third herself in Canva, and publishes. Total time from opening ChatGPT to a finished thumbnail: about 15 minutes, versus the 40 minutes she used to spend testing random prompts with no brief.

placeholders.name: Instagram / LinkedIn / TikTok / X / Facebook — name exactly one
placeholders.what: This tells the AI which single platform the caption is for — not a list, just one name copied from the options given. Pick the platform where the post will actually be published, because each one has a completely different reading pattern (LinkedIn readers scan for professional insight, TikTok viewers read captions as an afterthought to the video). A bad value is leaving multiple platforms in, like 'Instagram and Facebook' — that produces a generic caption that fits neither well.

LinkedIn
TikTok

placeholders.name: YOUR CONCEPT
placeholders.what: This is the specific idea or message the post is built around — not a topic, an actual angle. It comes from your content calendar or the raw idea you started with today. A bad value is a topic label like 'new product'; a good value is a full sentence describing what the post is actually saying, what changed, what the audience gets, or what the hook is.
examples: We just added oat milk as a permanent menu option after three months of customer requests — this post announces it and thanks people for asking.
Behind-the-scenes look at how our roastery sources beans directly from three family farms in Guatemala, tying it to our 'know your farmer' value.
A lighthearted post poking fun at the fact that our regulars now have a 'usual order' memorized by every barista on staff.

Pull this from a brand voice guide if one exists, or from how the brand's best-performing past captions actually read. A bad value is a vague word like 'professional' alone; a good value pairs tone words with a specific dos/don'ts.
examples: Warm and conversational, like texting a friend, never uses exclamation-point-heavy hype language
Confident and a little dry-humored, avoids emojis except sparingly, never says 'game-changer' or 'revolutionary'
Encouraging and plainspoken, avoids diet-culture phrases like 'guilt-free' or 'earn your workout'

placeholders.name: awareness / engagement / drive traffic / conversion
placeholders.what: State which single outcome this specific post is meant to achieve, chosen from the four listed. This shapes everything from the CTA to the hook — an awareness post can be looser and more shareable, a conversion post needs urgency and clarity. A bad value is picking more than one goal or leaving it blank; a good value is one word matching your actual campaign objective for this post.
examples: engagement
drive traffic
conversion

placeholders.name: WHAT YOU WANT THE READER TO DO
placeholders.what: The literal next action you want someone to take after reading, stated as an instruction, not a vague hope. This should match the goal above — if the goal is 'drive traffic,' the CTA should be a click action, not just 'like this post.' A bad value is something abstract like 'engage more'; a good value is a specific action tied to a specific destination.

Comment which farm's beans is your favorite so far
Save this post if you're planning a trip to try the new seasonal menu
