For each platform, respect its typical caption length, hook convention, and formatting norms (line breaks, hashtag placement and count, emoji use). Give 2 hook options per platform, then the full caption using the stronger one. Clearly label which caption is for which platform, and do not let one platform's phrasing bleed into the other.

variations.label: Short-form video script + caption combo
variations.whenToUse: Use this when writing for TikTok or Instagram Reels and you need the on-screen text/spoken hook for the video itself, not just the caption underneath it.
variations.prompt:
I'm writing a short-form video (TikTok/Reels), not just a caption. Give me both the video script and the caption.

Platform: [TikTok / Instagram Reels]
Post concept/core message: [YOUR CONCEPT]
Brand voice: [YOUR VOICE DESCRIPTION]
Goal: [awareness / engagement / drive traffic / conversion]
Call to action: [WHAT YOU WANT THE READER TO DO]

First, give me 3 opening-line hook options for the first 1-2 seconds of the video (spoken or on-screen text) — this is what determines whether someone keeps watching. Then write a beat-by-beat script (what's said/shown, roughly how many seconds each beat gets) using the strongest hook. Then write the caption that goes underneath, following TikTok/Reels caption conventions (short, casual, hashtags placed at the end, minimal formatting). The script and caption should reinforce each other, not repeat the same sentence twice.

variations.label: No hard CTA — pure engagement/community post
variations.whenToUse: Use this for posts that intentionally don't push toward a click or sale, like a community question, meme, or relatable moment, where a hard CTA would feel out of place.
variations.prompt:
Write a caption for a social media post.

Platform: [Instagram / LinkedIn / TikTok / X / Facebook — name exactly one]
Post concept/core message: [YOUR CONCEPT]
Brand voice: [YOUR VOICE DESCRIPTION]
Goal: engagement — specifically getting comments/shares, not clicks or sales

This post has no hard call to action — do not add a 'shop now' or 'link in bio' style push. Instead, end with something that naturally invites a comment (a question, a relatable statement, an 'agree or disagree' prompt) that fits the concept and voice. Write it for how people actually read on this platform — respect typical caption length, hook convention, and formatting norms. Give me 3 different hook/opening line options, then the full caption using the strongest one.

followUps.label: Tighten a caption that's running too long
followUps.prompt: This caption is longer than what actually performs on this platform. Cut it by about a third without losing the hook or the CTA — tighten sentences rather than deleting whole ideas.

followUps.label: Make the hashtags more specific
followUps.prompt: The hashtags feel generic and overused. Replace them with a mix of a couple of broad, high-volume tags and several narrower, more specific ones actually related to this post's content.

followUps.label: Check it against our brand voice more strictly
followUps.prompt: Re-read this caption against the brand voice I gave you and point out any word or phrase that doesn't actually match it, then rewrite just those parts.

followUps.label: Give me more hook options to test
followUps.prompt: Give me 3 more hook/opening line options I haven't seen yet, as different in approach from each other as possible, so I can test which one performs best.

smm-b2-platform-native-captions-hooks.walkthrough:
Jordan handles Instagram and LinkedIn for a small-batch coffee roastery and needs a caption today announcing that oat milk is now a permanent menu item after months of customer requests.

Jordan opens ChatGPT and pastes the lesson's prompt. For Platform, Jordan types "Instagram." For the concept: "We just added oat milk as a permanent menu option after three months of customer requests — this post announces it and thanks people for asking." For brand voice: "warm and conversational, like texting a friend, never uses exclamation-point-heavy hype language." Goal: "engagement." CTA: "comment which milk alternative we should add next."

ChatGPT returns three hook options, including "you asked. we listened. oat milk is here to stay" and "the most-requested menu change just became permanent," then builds the full caption around the second one, formatted with short line breaks, a warm middle section thanking regulars, the CTA question at the end, and five hashtags placed after a line break at the bottom — matching how Instagram captions actually get read.

Jordan likes the structure but notices the caption runs long for how their regulars typically skim captions on mobile, so Jordan sends the follow-up: "This caption is longer than what actually performs on this platform. Cut it by about a third without losing the hook or the CTA." ChatGPT trims two middle sentences and tightens the wording, keeping the hook and CTA intact.

Jordan copies the shortened caption straight into the scheduling tool. Total time from opening the prompt to having a ready-to-post caption: about 10 minutes, most of it spent deciding on the exact concept sentence rather than waiting on the AI.

placeholders.name: e.g., "warm, direct, a little playful, never use corporate phrases like 'we appreciate your feedback,' sign off with our first names when it fits"
placeholders.what: This describes exactly how the brand talks when responding to people directly — not the same as a general marketing voice, since replies are more personal and one-to-one. Pull this from an actual brand voice guide, or from real examples of past replies that got a good reaction. A bad value is a single adjective like 'friendly'; a good value includes tone words plus specific banned phrases and sign-off style, since those are what actually keep replies from sounding like a corporate copy-paste.
examples: Warm, direct, a little playful, never use corporate phrases like 'we appreciate your feedback' or 'thank you for reaching out,' sign off with our first names (Sam or Alex) when it fits naturally
Calm, precise, no exclamation points, never over-apologize for minor issues, always confirm next steps clearly rather than just sympathizing
Enthusiastic but not gushing, uses one emoji max per reply, avoids the word 'amazing,' always thanks people by referencing what they specifically said

placeholders.name: PASTE EACH COMMENT/DM, ONE PER LINE, NUMBERED
placeholders.what: This is the actual, unedited text of each comment or DM pulled from your platform's inbox or comment section — copied exactly as the person wrote it, numbered so the AI's replies map back to the right one. A bad value is paraphrasing what people said; a good value is the verbatim text, including typos, tone, and any details the person mentioned, since the AI needs those specifics to write a reply that responds to what was actually said.
examples:
1. love this!! do you ship to canada?
2. this didn't work for me at all, my order arrived broken and customer service hasn't answered in 4 days
3. can you do a tutorial on the technique you used in the last video?
4. following since day one, so proud of how far this account has grown
5. is this safe to use if I'm pregnant?
6. y'all are a scam, I'm reporting this page

1. what font is that in your last carousel?
2. just cancelled my subscription, this is way overpriced for what it is
3. can you tag the jacket she's wearing??
4. my daughter has severe allergies, does this product contain tree nuts?
5. lol relatable content as always
6. DM'd you 3 times about a refund and no response, this is ridiculous

variations.label: High-volume comment backlog (20+ items)
variations.whenToUse: Use this when clearing a large backlog of comments at once and you want them grouped by type instead of replied to one by one, so you can scan and approve faster.
variations.prompt:
Draft replies to this large batch of comments in our brand voice.

Brand voice guide: [YOUR VOICE GUIDE]

Comments (numbered):
[PASTE EACH COMMENT, ONE PER LINE, NUMBERED]

First, sort them into three groups: (1) straightforward replies you can draft directly, (2) comments similar enough to reply with near-identical wording (like repeated 'do you ship internationally' questions), and (3) comments to escalate. For group 1 and 2, write a specific reply for each numbered comment — group 2 replies can share a template but each must reference what that person actually asked. For group 3, write "ESCALATE" and briefly say why — this includes complaints, safety/legal concerns, sensitive personal situations, or anything angry or ambiguous enough that a wrong-toned reply could make it worse.

variations.label: DM-only, product/purchase questions
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a batch of direct messages that are mostly pre-purchase questions, where factual accuracy about the product matters more than tone alone.
variations.prompt:
Draft replies to this batch of DMs in our brand voice. These are mostly product questions from people considering a purchase, so accuracy matters as much as tone.

Brand voice guide: [YOUR VOICE GUIDE]
Facts you're allowed to state (only use these, don't infer product details I haven't given you): [PASTE KNOWN PRODUCT FACTS: pricing, shipping, ingredients/materials, policies]

DMs (numbered):
[PASTE EACH DM, ONE PER LINE, NUMBERED]

For each one, write a specific reply that answers what that person actually asked, using only the facts I gave you above — if a DM asks something you don't have facts for (like a specific allergen or a delivery date), don't guess, write "NEEDS INFO" and note exactly what's missing. Flag anything that should be escalated to a human instead — complaints, safety concerns, or refund/legal requests — with "ESCALATE" and a brief reason.

variations.label: Single high-stakes comment
variations.whenToUse: Use this when there's just one sensitive or semi-public comment that needs a careful, considered reply rather than a batch pass.
variations.prompt:
Help me think through how to respond to this one comment before I draft anything.

Brand voice guide: [YOUR VOICE GUIDE]
The comment: [PASTE THE FULL COMMENT TEXT]
Context I know: [WHAT YOU KNOW ABOUT THE SITUATION, e.g. "this customer's order actually was delayed by our carrier, we already know about it"]

First tell me plainly whether this is something you think should be escalated to a human rather than replied to directly — and if so, stop there and explain why rather than drafting a reply. If it's safe to draft, give me two versions: a short public reply (for the comment thread, assuming other people will see it) and, separately, a private DM I could send if I want to move the conversation off the public thread.

followUps.label: Shorten replies that read too formal or long
followUps.prompt: Several of these replies are longer and more formal than how we actually talk to people. Tighten them to match a real conversational reply length for this platform, without losing what makes each one specific to that comment.

followUps.label: Double-check the escalation calls
followUps.prompt: Go back through the ones you marked as regular replies (not ESCALATE) and double-check each one — are any of them actually ambiguous, sensitive, or risky enough that they should have been flagged? Explain your reasoning for any you change.

followUps.label: Match our specific phrasing quirks more closely
followUps.prompt: These sound close to our voice but not quite right. We always sign off with a first name when replying to a direct question, and we never use the word 'awesome.' Revise the drafts to fix that.

followUps.label: Write escalation notes for whoever picks these up
followUps.prompt: For each comment you marked ESCALATE, write a one-line internal note for the teammate who will handle it — what happened, what tone/response it likely needs, and any urgency flag.

smm-i1-engagement-replies-brand-voice.walkthrough:
Priya works at a small agency handling comment moderation for a skincare brand's Instagram account, and Monday mornings mean clearing the weekend's backlog of comments and DMs before the brand's founder checks in at 10am.

She opens Claude and pastes the lesson's prompt. For brand voice, she pastes: "warm, direct, a little playful, never use corporate phrases like we appreciate your feedback, sign off with our first names when it fits." Then she copies six real comments straight from the Instagram app into the numbered list — including a simple shipping question, a compliment, a tutorial request, and one comment that reads: "this broke me out badly, my skin is still irritated three days later, is this even tested properly?"

Claude drafts short, specific replies for five of the comments — the shipping question gets a real answer about international shipping, the tutorial request gets a reply pointing to a saved highlight. For the breakout comment, Claude writes "ESCALATE — this describes a possible adverse skin reaction; a wrong-toned reply could look dismissive of a safety concern, and this needs a human who can ask for details and involve the team if needed," with no drafted reply.

Priya reads through and thinks a couple of the 'safe' replies still sound slightly too formal for how this brand actually talks, so she sends the follow-up: "These sound close to our voice but not quite right — we never use the word amazing. Revise the drafts to fix that." Claude adjusts the wording.

Priya posts the five approved replies directly and forwards the escalated comment to the brand's customer care lead with the note Claude drafted attached. Total time: about 12 minutes for a backlog that used to take her half an hour.

placeholders.name: DATE RANGE
placeholders.what: The specific start and end dates this report covers, matching whatever period your analytics tool exported (weekly, monthly, or a campaign window). This anchors every comparison the AI makes, so be exact rather than vague. A bad value is 'last month'; a good value is the actual dates as shown in your analytics dashboard.
examples: July 1 - July 31, 2026
Week of August 3-9, 2026
Q2 2026 (April 1 - June 30)

placeholders.name: PASTE: reach, impressions, engagement rate, follower change, top 3 posts by performance, bottom 3 posts by performance, any other metrics tracked
placeholders.what: The actual numbers pulled from your platform's native analytics or a reporting tool, not rounded guesses or a memory of how the month felt. Include the prior period's numbers too if you want the AI to compare trends, since it can't invent a comparison you didn't give it. A bad value is a vague summary like 'engagement was up'; a good value is the raw figures with labels, including which specific posts were the top and bottom performers and why (format, topic).
examples:
Reach: 84,200 (prior period: 71,500)
Impressions: 211,000 (prior: 198,300)
Engagement rate: 4.1% (prior: 3.4%)
Follower change: +312 (prior: +190)
Top 3 posts: (1) Carousel 'behind the scenes at our farm' - 6,100 likes, 340 comments (2) Reel 'day in the life' - 5,800 likes (3) Static 'customer testimonial' - 3,200 likes
Bottom 3 posts: (1) Static product photo, no caption hook - 210 likes (2) Repost of press mention - 180 likes (3) Poll story with low response

Reach: 12,400 (prior: 15,900)
Impressions: 29,000 (prior: 33,500)
Engagement rate: 2.1% (prior: 2.8%)
Follower change: +45 (prior: +120)
Top 3 posts: LinkedIn article on industry trend (890 reactions), customer case study post (410 reactions), team hire announcement (380 reactions)
Bottom 3 posts: generic product update (22 reactions), repost of a stat graphic (18 reactions), event recap posted 2 weeks late (15 reactions)

placeholders.name: PASTE: campaigns run, posting frequency or format changes, external events, platform changes you're aware of — or write "none known"
placeholders.what: Anything you actually know happened during this period that could plausibly explain a change in the numbers — a paid campaign, a change in how often you posted, a holiday, a platform outage, an algorithm change you read about from an official source. This is the only material the AI is allowed to use for explanations, so leaving it out forces the report to stay purely factual. If you genuinely don't know of anything, write 'none known' rather than leaving it blank.
examples: Ran a paid boost on the 'behind the scenes at our farm' carousel for 5 days ($200 budget). Posted 2 more times per week than the prior period. No known platform changes. Instagram had a widely reported outage on July 14 for about 3 hours.
none known
Switched from posting daily to 4x/week starting mid-month to focus more on quality. Ran a LinkedIn ad campaign promoting the webinar from July 10-20. No external events we're aware of.

variations.label: Multi-platform combined report
variations.whenToUse: Use this when reporting across more than one platform in a single document instead of just one, so leadership or a client can see the whole picture at once.
variations.prompt:
Turn these analytics numbers into a report explaining what happened this period, across multiple platforms.

Period: [DATE RANGE]
Instagram numbers: [PASTE METRICS]
TikTok numbers: [PASTE METRICS]
LinkedIn numbers: [PASTE METRICS]
Known context (things that actually happened this period): [PASTE CONTEXT OR "none known"]

Write the report with a platform-by-platform breakdown, each following the same two-section structure: (1) "What happened" — a factual summary of the numbers only, comparing to the prior period if given, no interpretation, and (2) "Possible explanations" — grounded hypotheses connecting only to context I actually gave you or patterns visible in the numbers, clearly labeled as hypotheses. End with a short cross-platform summary noting where platforms moved in the same direction vs. diverged. If you don't have enough context to explain a change on any platform, say so directly instead of guessing.

variations.label: Quick internal weekly check-in
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a fast, informal update to your own team, such as a Slack message, rather than a formal client-facing report.
variations.prompt:
Turn these numbers into a short, informal weekly check-in for my team — this is going in Slack, not to a client, so keep it brief and conversational rather than formal.

Period: [DATE RANGE]
Numbers: [PASTE METRICS]
Known context: [PASTE CONTEXT OR "none known"]

Give me 4-6 bullet points total: what moved (up or down, with the number), and only where I've given you context or a visible pattern in the numbers, a short grounded guess at why — label any guess clearly as a guess. If a number moved and I haven't given you anything to explain it, just say it moved and that the cause is unclear, don't speculate.

variations.label: Quarterly rollup for leadership
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a longer, higher-level report covering a full quarter, meant for people who care about overall trend direction more than individual post performance.
variations.prompt:
Turn these analytics numbers into a quarterly report explaining what happened, written for leadership who care about overall trend, not individual post details.

Period: [DATE RANGE, e.g. Q3 2026]
Monthly numbers for each month in the quarter: [PASTE: reach, impressions, engagement rate, follower change per month]
Known context (campaigns, strategy changes, external events across the quarter): [PASTE CONTEXT OR "none known"]

Write the report in two sections: (1) "What happened" — the quarter-over-quarter and month-over-month trend in each metric, factually, no interpretation, and (2) "Possible explanations" — grounded hypotheses for the trend, connected only to context I actually gave you, clearly labeled as hypotheses rather than facts. Close with one short paragraph on what to watch next quarter, based only on patterns actually shown in this data.

followUps.label: Double-check for unsupported causal claims
followUps.prompt: Re-read the 'Possible explanations' section and point out anywhere it states a cause more confidently than the evidence supports. Rewrite those lines to be clearly hedged or move them to a 'not enough context to explain' note.

followUps.label: Add a short executive summary at the top
followUps.prompt: Add a 2-3 sentence plain-English summary at the very top of this report — the headline takeaway a busy client would want if they only read one paragraph. Keep it factual, don't introduce new interpretation that isn't already in the report below.

followUps.label: Turn findings into next-period recommendations
followUps.prompt: Based only on what's in the 'What happened' and 'Possible explanations' sections above, suggest 3 concrete things to try next period. Don't introduce new strategic ideas that aren't grounded in what we actually observed this period.

followUps.label: Shorten for a client with limited time
followUps.prompt: This is too long for this client — they only skim reports. Cut it to about half the length, keeping the two-section structure and the fact-vs-hypothesis distinction, but trim to only the highest-impact numbers and explanations.

smm-i2-analytics-narratives.walkthrough:
Tomas manages social for a client's outdoor apparel brand and owes them a monthly report by Friday explaining July's performance, including why engagement jumped compared to June.

He opens ChatGPT and pastes the lesson's prompt. For the period, he types "July 1 - July 31, 2026." For numbers, he pastes the export from Instagram's native analytics: reach, impressions, engagement rate, follower change, and the top and bottom three posts with their exact like and comment counts, noting the top post was a behind-the-scenes carousel. For known context, he writes that they ran a five-day paid boost on that carousel, increased posting frequency by two posts a week compared to June, and that Instagram had a documented three-hour outage on July 14.

ChatGPT returns a report with a "What happened" section stating the raw numbers and comparisons to June with no interpretation, followed by "Possible explanations," which notes: "The top-performing post was a carousel, and carousels also outperformed other formats last period — this suggests the format itself may be a factor (hypothesis)." It also flags that a reach dip on July 14 aligns with the reported outage that day, labeled as a hypothesis based on timing, and explicitly states it doesn't have enough context to explain the follower growth rate beyond noting it tracks with increased posting frequency.

Tomas wants to be extra careful before sending it to the client, so he sends the follow-up asking ChatGPT to re-check the explanations section for anything stated too confidently. It flags one line that implied the paid boost caused the whole engagement jump rather than just the top post, and softens it.

He adds the executive-summary follow-up, then sends the final report. Total time: about 30 minutes.

placeholders.name: ONE SENTENCE, e.g. "summer product launch, bright and energetic"
placeholders.what: A single sentence naming the campaign and its overall mood — this is the anchor idea every visual in the set needs to share. Pull this from your campaign brief or come up with it based on what the campaign is actually promoting. A bad value is a vague word like 'fun'; a good value names what's being promoted plus 2-3 mood words.
examples: fall sweater restock, cozy and warm-toned
back-to-school supply bundle, bright and organized-feeling
10-year anniversary sale, celebratory and a little nostalgic

placeholders.name: YOUR EXACT COLORS/HEX CODES
placeholders.what: The literal hex codes or precise color names from your brand guidelines, not a general description like 'blue.' Find these in your brand style guide, past design files, or by asking whoever manages brand assets. A bad value is 'our brand colors'; a good value lists exact hex codes so every generated image actually matches, since both GPT Image 2 and Gemini's native generation can drift in color without this.
examples: #2D5A3D (forest green), #F4E9D8 (cream), #C9622B (rust orange)
#1A1A2E (near-black navy), #E94560 (coral red), #FFFFFF (white) — no other colors allowed
#7C9885 (sage), #F7F3E9 (off-white), #3D3D3D (charcoal, text/dark elements only)

placeholders.name: e.g., "flat vector illustration style, bold color blocking, one clear subject, minimal detail, no gradients"
placeholders.what: A precise description of the visual style ChatGPT or Gemini should render in, specific enough that you can paste this exact wording again for every future image and get a matching look. Base this on an existing brand style if one exists, or decide it now and treat it as fixed for the whole campaign. A bad value is 'nice looking image'; a good value names the rendering technique, level of detail, and what to avoid.
examples: flat vector illustration style, bold color blocking, one clear subject, minimal detail, no gradients, no drop shadows
warm natural photography style, soft daylight, shallow depth of field, single product in focus, no studio lighting look
hand-drawn line art style, single-weight black outlines, one flat accent color fill, no shading, no background texture

placeholders.name: WHAT SHOULD BE SHOWN
placeholders.what: The specific subject of this particular visual — what a viewer should see when they look at it. This changes for every image in the set even though the style and colors stay fixed. A bad value is something abstract like 'the brand feeling'; a good value describes a concrete subject and its pose or arrangement.
examples: a single knit sweater laid flat at an angle, sleeve slightly folded
a backpack standing upright with a few school supplies spilling out beside it, arranged neatly
a birthday cake with a single lit candle, viewed from a slight overhead angle

placeholders.name: FORMAT, e.g. "a square 1:1 feed image" / "a vertical 9:16 story image" / "a wide banner"
placeholders.what: The exact dimensions or aspect ratio and platform placement this specific image is for, since composition needs to change with the format — a story image needs vertical breathing room, a banner needs horizontal focal balance. Check this against where the image will actually be used, such as Instagram feed vs. Story vs. a website hero. A bad value is 'normal size'; a good value names the aspect ratio and its use.
examples: a square 1:1 feed image
a vertical 9:16 story image
a wide 3:1 website banner

variations.label: Photography-style instead of illustration
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the brand's existing visual identity is photo-based rather than illustrated, and ChatGPT or Gemini needs to mimic a photographic look consistently.
variations.prompt:
Generate a set of campaign visuals that need to look like one consistent campaign across formats, in a photographic style.

Campaign theme: [ONE SENTENCE]
Brand colors: [YOUR EXACT COLORS/HEX CODES]
Style description (I will reuse this exact wording for every format): [e.g., "natural daylight photography, shallow depth of field, warm color grading, single product or subject in sharp focus, softly blurred background"]
Subject/concept for this visual: [WHAT SHOULD BE SHOWN]

Generate this as: [FORMAT], with a clear focal point and negative space suitable for a text overlay I'll add separately.

Avoid: in-image text, any color cast outside my stated palette, studio-lighting look if I specified natural light, a different depth of field or angle than what I specified.

After this one, I'll ask for the same style description in a different format/dimension — keep the style description identical each time so the set matches.

variations.label: Quote/testimonial card with baked-in text
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a testimonial or quote graphic where the text is part of the visual design itself and needs to be generated or laid out as part of the image, not added afterward.
variations.prompt:
Generate a quote/testimonial card graphic for this campaign.

Campaign theme: [ONE SENTENCE]
Brand colors: [YOUR EXACT COLORS/HEX CODES]
Style description (reuse this exact wording for every card in the set): [YOUR STYLE DESCRIPTION]
Quote text to feature: [EXACT QUOTE TEXT AND ATTRIBUTION]

Generate this as: [FORMAT], designed with the quote text as the central visual element — clear, legible typography treatment consistent with the brand style, generous margins around the text, no competing imagery that would make the quote hard to read.

Avoid: any color outside my stated palette, a busy background that reduces legibility, a different rendering style than specified.

Since exact typography may not render perfectly, tell me if I should expect to need to redo the text in a design tool afterward, and if so, describe the background/layout in enough detail that I can recreate it.

variations.label: Icon set for Highlight covers or small repeated motifs
variations.whenToUse: Use this when generating a small set of simple repeated icons, like Instagram Highlight covers, rather than full campaign scenes.
variations.prompt:
Generate a set of simple icon-style images that need to look like one consistent set.

Brand colors: [YOUR EXACT COLORS/HEX CODES]
Style description (I will reuse this exact wording for every icon): [e.g., "single-line minimal icon, one color fill, centered on a plain circular background, no text, no shading"]
Icon subject for this one: [WHAT SHOULD BE SHOWN, e.g. "a coffee cup"]

Generate this as: a square 1:1 image sized for use as a small icon (will be cropped into a circle).

Avoid: any color outside my stated palette, added background elements, inconsistent line weight from icon to icon, any text.

After this one, I'll ask for more icons in the same set using this exact style description — keep it identical each time so the icons look like a matched set.

followUps.label: Fix an off-palette color
followUps.prompt: The background came out in a color that's not in my palette. Regenerate this using only [YOUR EXACT COLORS/HEX CODES] — no other colors, including no unintended tints or gradients between them.

followUps.label: Improve negative space for text overlay
followUps.prompt: There isn't enough clear, uncluttered space for me to add a text overlay afterward. Regenerate this with a larger area of flat negative space in the top third, keeping the subject and style otherwise the same.

followUps.label: Fix style drift from the rest of the set
followUps.prompt: This one doesn't match the rendering style of the other images in this set — it looks more detailed and shaded than the flat, minimal look of the others. Regenerate it using exactly this style description again: [YOUR STYLE DESCRIPTION], matching the others as closely as possible.

followUps.label: Get focal-point options to choose from
followUps.prompt: Generate 3 variations of this same image with different focal point placement or subject arrangement, keeping the same style description and color palette, so I can pick the one with the best composition.

smm-i3-campaign-visuals-ai-image.walkthrough:
Renee is launching a plant-based snack brand's back-to-school campaign and needs a matching square feed image and vertical story image before the campaign goes live Monday.

She opens ChatGPT and pastes the lesson's prompt, since GPT Image 2 is her default for anything needing precise brand-color matching. Campaign theme: "back-to-school snack bundle, bright and organized-feeling." Brand colors: "#4A7C59 (green), #F2C14E (yellow), #FFFFFF (white)." Style description: "flat vector illustration style, bold color blocking, one clear subject, minimal detail, no gradients." Subject: "a lunchbox open on a table with three snack bars arranged neatly inside." Format: "a square 1:1 feed image."

The result mostly matches, but the background has a subtle gradient behind the lunchbox instead of a flat color, and a small doodle of a pencil that wasn't requested. Renee sends a follow-up: "The background came out with a gradient, not flat color. Regenerate using only #4A7C59, #F2C14E, #FFFFFF — no gradients, and remove the pencil doodle." The correction fixes both issues.

For the story format, she considers switching to Gemini to try its conversational editing, but decides to stay in the same ChatGPT thread instead, since the lesson warns that switching tools mid-campaign risks drift even with the same wording. She pastes the identical style description and colors, changing only the format line to "a vertical 9:16 story image" and the subject to "the same lunchbox, cropped closer with more empty space above for a headline." The result matches the feed image's style closely, but the focal point sits a little low.

She sends the negative-space follow-up, asking for more flat space in the top third. The revised version works. Total time for both finished visuals: about 15 minutes, most of it spent on the two correction rounds rather than the initial generation.

placeholders.name: PASTE FOR EACH CLIENT: name, 3-5 tone words, phrases/words they never use, typical CTA style, any hard rules (e.g., "never mentions competitors by name")
placeholders.what: This is the actual voice profile for every client you manage, listed one after another — pulled from each client's brand guidelines, kickoff notes, or your own observations from past approved content. A bad value is one vague line per client like 'client A is friendly'; a good value gives each client a name, several specific tone words, banned words/phrases, how they like CTAs phrased, and any hard rule that would be a real problem if broken.
examples:
CLIENT: Northstar Dental. Tone: warm, reassuring, plainspoken, family-friendly, never clinical-sounding. Never use: 'procedure' (say 'visit' instead), never use fear-based language about pain. CTA style: soft, always frames booking as easy, e.g. 'grab a spot that works for you.' Hard rule: never post patient photos without a signed release on file.

CLIENT: Ridgeline Outdoor Gear. Tone: rugged, confident, minimal, a little dry-humored. Never use: exclamation points, the word 'adventure' (overused in the category). CTA style: direct and short, e.g. 'shop the drop.' Hard rule: never mentions competitor brands by name, even to compare favorably.

CLIENT: Bloom & Co Florist. Tone: gentle, poetic but not overwrought, seasonal. Never use: 'affordable' or any price-focused language (positioned as premium). CTA style: invitational, e.g. 'stop by and see what's blooming.' Hard rule: always credit the specific flower variety by name, never just say 'flowers.'

CLIENT: Vantage Legal Group. Tone: authoritative, calm, precise, zero humor. Never use: contractions (write 'do not' not 'don't'), never use emojis. CTA style: formal, e.g. 'contact our office for a consultation.' Hard rule: never state a legal outcome as guaranteed.

placeholders.name: PASTE FOR EACH CLIENT: what needs sign-off before posting, who approves it, typical turnaround
placeholders.what: The actual approval process for each client — what kind of content needs a human sign-off before it goes live, the specific person's name or role who approves it, and how long that usually takes. This comes from your contract or working agreement with each client, not a guess. A bad value is 'they like to review things'; a good value states exactly what needs approval, who the approver is by name/role, and a realistic turnaround time.
examples:
Northstar Dental: all posts need approval, approver is Dr. Patel (practice owner), turnaround usually 24 hours but can be 48 hours on weekends.
Ridgeline Outdoor Gear: only paid/promotional posts need approval, approver is Casey (marketing director), turnaround same-day usually.

Bloom & Co Florist: only posts mentioning pricing or promotions need approval, approver is owner Maritza, turnaround 1-2 days.
Vantage Legal Group: every single post needs approval before posting, approver is the managing partner's assistant Renee who routes it to the partner, turnaround 3-5 business days — plan ahead.

variations.label: Two-client minimal starter version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you're a freelancer just starting out with two clients and want a lighter system to build the habit before scaling to more accounts.
variations.prompt:
Help me build a simple two-client system that prevents me from mixing up brand voice or missing approvals.

My two clients and their voice profiles:
[PASTE FOR EACH CLIENT: name, 3-5 tone words, phrases/words they never use, typical CTA style, any hard rules]

Approval requirements per client:
[PASTE FOR EACH CLIENT: what needs sign-off, who approves it, typical turnaround]

Build just three things, kept as simple as possible since I'm doing this solo: (1) a one-page voice card per client, identical format for both so I can compare at a glance, (2) one standing rule to put at the top of every prompt I write — always name the exact client first and check the draft against their card before sending anything, and (3) a 5-item pre-send checklist starting with confirming which client this is for. Don't build an approval-tracking system yet — I don't need it with just two clients.

variations.label: Adding a new client to an existing system
variations.whenToUse: Use this once the system already exists and you're onboarding one additional client, so you extend the system instead of rebuilding it from scratch.
variations.prompt:
I already have a multi-client voice-card and approval-tracking system for my other clients. I'm adding one new client and want their card and approval entry to match the existing format exactly.

Here's the format my existing voice cards use: [PASTE ONE EXISTING VOICE CARD AS A TEMPLATE EXAMPLE]

New client's voice profile: [PASTE: name, 3-5 tone words, phrases/words they never use, typical CTA style, any hard rules]
New client's approval requirements: [PASTE: what needs sign-off, who approves it, typical turnaround]

Build a voice card for this new client in the exact same format/structure as my existing one, and a new row/entry for my approval-tracking log in the same format. Also tell me if anything about this client's voice is similar enough to one of my other clients that I should add an explicit contrast note to avoid mixing them up — [NAME YOUR OTHER SIMILAR CLIENT(S) IF ANY].

variations.label: Managing multiple owned brands instead of agency clients
variations.whenToUse: Use this if you're not an agency managing external clients but you personally run more than one brand or page, such as a personal brand plus a side business, and need the same mix-up prevention.
variations.prompt:
Help me build a system that prevents me from mixing up voice or missing steps across the multiple brands/pages I personally run.

My brands and their voice profiles:
[PASTE FOR EACH BRAND: name, 3-5 tone words, phrases/words never used, typical CTA style, any hard rules]

My own review process per brand (since I'm approving my own content, this is about catching mistakes, not client sign-off):
[PASTE FOR EACH BRAND: what you personally double-check before posting, e.g. "always re-read against the voice card," "check I didn't cross-post the wrong brand's content to the wrong account"]

Build: (1) a one-page voice-profile reference card per brand, identical format across all so I can compare quickly, (2) a standing rule to put at the top of every prompt — always name which brand this is for before asking for content, (3) a pre-send checklist starting with confirming which brand's account I'm about to post to, since cross-posting to the wrong account is my biggest real risk, and (4) a simple log format to track what's drafted, posted, and when per brand. Keep all of it simple enough I'll actually use it daily.

followUps.label: Add a new client without rebuilding everything
followUps.prompt: I'm adding a new client called [CLIENT NAME]. Here's their voice profile and approval process: [PASTE VOICE PROFILE AND APPROVAL DETAILS]. Build just their voice card and approval-log entry in the exact same format as the others above — don't change the format of my existing clients' cards.

followUps.label: Make the voice cards more scannable
followUps.prompt: These voice cards are a little too long for me to scan quickly when I'm switching between clients fast. Condense each one to fit in about 8-10 lines max, keeping the tone words, banned phrases, CTA style, and hard rules, but tightening the wording.

followUps.label: Flag clients whose voices could get confused with each other
followUps.prompt: Look at all the voice cards you've built and tell me which clients have similar enough tone words or styles that I could realistically mix them up under time pressure. For those specific pairs, add a short 'don't confuse with X' contrast note to each card.

followUps.label: Turn the approval log into a reusable weekly template
followUps.prompt: Turn the approval-tracking format into a blank weekly template I can copy and reuse every week, with the client names already filled in as row headers and empty cells for status, date, and notes.

smm-a1-multi-client-workflows.walkthrough:
Dana is a freelance social media manager with four clients — a dental practice, an outdoor gear brand, a florist, and a law firm — and last month she accidentally posted a casual, joke-filled caption meant for the outdoor brand onto the law firm's account before catching it in the scheduler. She wants a system that makes that impossible going forward.

She opens Claude and pastes the lesson's prompt. In the first bracket she pastes four short profiles, one per client: name, tone words, banned phrases, CTA style, and hard rules — for the law firm, she includes 'never use contractions, never state a legal outcome as guaranteed.' In the second bracket she pastes each client's approval process: who signs off and how long it takes, noting the law firm needs 3-5 business days because it routes through a partner's assistant.

Claude returns four identically formatted one-page voice cards, a standing rule to paste at the top of every future prompt ('always name the exact client before asking for content'), a five-item pre-send checklist starting with 'confirm which client this is for and open their voice card,' and a simple table for tracking draft, approved, and posted status per client.

Reading it over, Dana realizes two of her clients — the florist and the dental practice — both use a 'warm and gentle' tone, which is exactly the kind of pair she could mix up. She sends the follow-up asking Claude to flag confusable clients and add contrast notes. Claude adds a line to each card: 'Bloom & Co is poetic and seasonal; Northstar Dental is plainspoken and reassuring — don't blend the two.'

She pins all four cards and the checklist in a doc she reuses daily. Total time: about 25 minutes.
